title: Predict the merge
prompt:

The two branches touched different files. You run `git merge projects-grid`. What does the graph look like afterwards?
hints: Which branch is HEAD on? That's the only branch that can move.
Has `main` gained commits since `projects-grid` split off at `b2`?
When both sides have new commits, a fast-forward is impossible.
explanation: HEAD is on `main`, so `main` is the branch that moves. Both branches have commits since their merge base `b2` (`c3` on `main`; `d4` and `e5` on `projects-grid`), so a fast-forward is impossible. Git does a three-way merge from `b2` and records a new merge commit whose parents are `c3` and `e5`. `main` moves to it; `projects-grid` stays on `e5` until you delete it.

a.text: `main` fast-forwards to `e5`; no new commit is made.
a.why: A fast-forward needs `main` to be an ancestor of `e5`. `c3` isn't in `projects-grid`'s history, so Git can't slide `main` along a straight line.

b.text: A new merge commit with parents `c3` and `e5` appears; `main` moves to it and `projects-grid` stays on `e5`.
b.why: Correct. Both sides moved since `b2`, so Git creates a two-parent commit on the current branch only.

c.text: A new merge commit appears and both `main` and `projects-grid` move to it.
c.why: Only the branch you're on moves during a merge. `projects-grid` keeps pointing at `e5`.

d.text: `d4` and `e5` are copied after `c3` with new IDs, keeping history linear.
d.why: That's what a rebase does. A merge keeps the original commits and joins the two lines with a merge commit.
